Section 1
HorizonCare Employee Health Plan is a fictional synthetic policy created for dRAGn retrieval
demonstrations. It intentionally contains numerical limits, waiting periods, exclusions, claim deadlines,
and exceptions that require precise retrieval.
At-a-glance figures
 • Hospitalization family-floater limit: ₹5,00,000.
 • Hospitalization deductible: ₹10,000.
 • Hospitalization co-payment: 10% after deductible.
 • Outpatient annual limit: ₹15,000 with 20% member share.
 • Maternity annual limit: ₹75,000 with 10% member share.
 • Pre-existing disease waiting period: 12 months.
 • Maternity waiting period: 9 months.

• Pre-existing disease waiting period: 12 months.
 • Maternity waiting period: 9 months.
 
Operational scenario
A new employee reaches the 30-day eligibility point but has not completed enrollment. Eligibility and
enrollment are related but not identical: coverage normally begins after the eligibility date and completion of
the enrollment process. A spouse or child added after a qualifying life event should use the applicable
special-enrollment window. A dependent child remains covered until the end of the month in which they
reach age 25, subject to dependency rules.
Interpretation and operational notes

reach age 25, subject to dependency rules.
Interpretation and operational notes
Health-plan questions should be answered by identifying the benefit category before looking for a numerical
limit. Hospitalization, outpatient consultation, prescription medicines, mental health services, ambulance,
maternity, and day-care treatment have different rules. The ₹5,00,000 hospitalization limit is a family-floater
balance, while the ₹75,000 maternity limit applies to the maternity benefit. Returning the largest number
simply because it appears in the document would therefore produce an incorrect answer.

simply because it appears in the document would therefore produce an incorrect answer.
Financial responsibility also has multiple layers. The ₹10,000 hospitalization deductible is a fixed annual
amount, while the 10% hospitalization member share is a percentage applied after the deductible.
Outpatient treatment uses a 20% member share and does not reduce the hospitalization deductible. Room
eligibility is separate again, with a ₹6,000 per-day room limit. A correct answer should preserve these
distinctions instead of combining them into one generic co-payment statement.
Claim questions also depend on timing and provider status. Planned hospitalization should normally be

pre-authorized 48 hours before admission, while emergency hospitalization should be reported within 24
hours. Reimbursement claims should normally be filed within 30 days of discharge. Network hospitals can
provide cashless service subject to authorization; eligible non-network treatment may be reimbursed but is
generally paid by the member first. These rules can interact, so retrieval should include enough surrounding
context to preserve the condition.
Waiting periods and exclusions are independent from network status. A treatment performed at a network
hospital can still be excluded, and a pre-existing condition can still be subject to its waiting period. Maternity

has a nine-month waiting period, pre-existing diseases have a 12-month waiting period, and specified
procedures have a 12-month waiting period. Accidental injury is treated differently and has no general
waiting period from the effective date. This makes the document useful for testing conditional retrieval and
citation accuracy.

1. Eligibility and Enrollment
Employee eligibility
 • Employees become eligible after 30 days of continuous employment unless their employment letter
 states otherwise.
• Coverage normally begins after enrollment is completed and the eligibility date is reached.
 
Dependents
 • Spouses and dependent children may be enrolled during annual enrollment or within 30 days of a
 qualifying life event.
• Dependent children are covered until the end of the month in which they reach age 25, subject to
 dependency rules.
Changes
A marriage, birth, adoption, or other qualifying life event may create a special enrollment opportunity.

Employees should provide the required documentation within the specified enrollment window.
Operational scenario

family-floater balance, so the first claim reduces what remains for other covered family members during the
policy year. This is different from the ₹75,000 maternity limit and the ₹15,000 outpatient limit. A correct
answer must identify the benefit category before selecting a number.

3. Deductibles, Co-payment and Room Limits
Deductible
 • The annual hospitalization deductible is ₹10,000 for the family floater.
 • The deductible is satisfied before eligible hospitalization coverage applies.
 
Co-payment
 • A 10% co-payment applies to eligible hospitalization expenses after the deductible.
 • Outpatient claims have a 20% member share and do not reduce the hospitalization deductible.
 
Room
 • Room charges are covered up to ₹6,000 per day.
 • Selecting a room above ₹6,000 per day may result in proportionate deductions to related hospital
 charges.

charges.
The deductible and co-payment should not be confused: the deductible is an initial amount, while the
co-payment is a percentage applied afterward.
Operational scenario
A patient is admitted for an emergency at night. The normal pre-authorization rule for planned
hospitalization is 48 hours before admission, but emergency hospitalization should instead be reported
within 24 hours. A treatment lasting less than 24 hours can still qualify when it is an approved day-care
procedure. Pre-authorization is a review of the proposed treatment; it is not a guarantee that every final bill
item will be paid.

4. Hospitalization and Day-care
 • Planned hospitalization should normally be pre-authorized at least 48 hours before admission.
 • Emergency hospitalization should be reported within 24 hours of admission.
 • Hospitalization normally requires at least 24 continuous hours unless the procedure is an approved
 day-care treatment.
Day-care
An approved procedure can qualify as day-care even without a 24-hour admission when it appears in the
approved procedure schedule and satisfies the policy conditions.
Authorization scenario
Pre-authorization confirms that the administrator has reviewed the proposed treatment; it does not

Pre-authorization confirms that the administrator has reviewed the proposed treatment; it does not
guarantee payment of every final expense. Final claims remain subject to eligibility, limits, exclusions,
documentation, and actual treatment.
Operational scenario
A member asks whether a condition diagnosed during the first few months of coverage is covered. The
answer depends on whether it is pre-existing and whether the applicable waiting period has expired. The
policy gives pre-existing diseases a 12-month waiting period and maternity a 9-month waiting period.
Accidental injury is treated differently and has no general waiting period from the effective date. Waiting

periods must therefore be read by condition, not as one universal rule.

6. Exclusions
 • Cosmetic procedures are excluded unless medically necessary following an accidental injury or
 covered reconstruction.
• Experimental or unproven treatments are excluded unless explicitly approved by the insurer.
 • Expenses caused by deliberate self-injury are excluded.
 • Non-prescription wellness supplements are not covered under prescription medicine benefits.
 • Personal comfort items, television charges, and non-medical attendant expenses are not covered.
 • Treatment that is not medically necessary or outside an eligible benefit category may be rejected.
 
Why exclusions matter

Why exclusions matter
A treatment may occur in a network hospital and still be excluded. Network status, medical necessity,
benefit category, and policy limits are separate checks.

after which the hospital submits the pre-authorization request. For reimbursement, the member submits the
claim form, discharge summary, itemized bills, prescriptions, payment proof, and required medical records.
Reimbursement claims should normally be filed within 30 days of discharge. Missing documents can pause

7. Claims and Pre-authorization
Cashless process
 • Present the health card and identity document at a network hospital.
 • The hospital sends a pre-authorization request to the claims administrator.
 • Treatment proceeds after authorization subject to the approved amount and policy conditions.
 
Reimbursement process
 • Submit the claim form, discharge summary, itemized bills, prescriptions, payment proof, and required
 medical records.
• Reimbursement claims should normally be submitted within 30 days of discharge.
 • Missing documents may pause processing until the requested information is supplied.

• Missing documents may pause processing until the requested information is supplied.
 Members should retain copies of all submitted documents and claim references so that later queries can
be resolved efficiently.
Operational scenario
A member receives treatment at a non-network hospital during an emergency. The treatment may still be
eligible for reimbursement, but it is generally not cashless and the member normally pays the hospital first.
Maternity has a separate ₹75,000 annual limit and a 9-month waiting period. A newborn should be added
within 30 days when the enrollment rule applies. These conditions should be checked separately rather than

assuming one hospital rule covers everything.

8. Network Hospitals and Maternity
Network
 • Cashless service is available only at participating network hospitals.
 • Non-network eligible treatment may be reimbursed, but the member normally pays the hospital first.
 • Emergency treatment at a non-network hospital remains subject to notification and policy
 requirements.
Maternity
 • Maternity coverage is limited to ₹75,000 per policy year.
 • Normal delivery and medically necessary cesarean delivery are eligible within the maternity limit.
 • Maternity has a 9-month waiting period unless a documented exception applies.

• Maternity has a 9-month waiting period unless a documented exception applies.
 • A newborn should be added within 30 days when the enrollment rule applies.
 
Operational scenario
A mental-health claim can be eligible up to ₹25,000 per year with a 10% member share, while general
wellness coaching or gym membership is outside the medical benefit. A ₹7,000 room exceeds the ₹6,000
daily room limit. A pre-existing disease during the first 12 months may be subject to the waiting period, and
a reimbursement claim filed 45 days after discharge is outside the normal 30-day window. Each outcome
depends on a different policy clause.

9. Mental Health and Common Claim Scenarios
Mental health
 • Eligible mental health treatment is covered up to ₹25,000 per year with a 10% member share.
 • General lifestyle coaching, gym memberships, and non-medical wellness programs are not covered
 under the medical benefit.
Scenarios
A ₹7,000 room exceeds the ₹6,000 eligible room limit and may trigger proportionate deductions. A
non-network hospital may be reimbursable but is generally not cashless. A pre-existing disease claim
during the first 12 months may be subject to the waiting period. A reimbursement claim submitted 45

during the first 12 months may be subject to the waiting period. A reimbursement claim submitted 45
days after discharge is outside the normal 30-day filing window and may require an exception.
Operational scenario
The most useful quick-reference numbers are ₹5,00,000 for hospitalization, ₹10,000 for the hospitalization
deductible, ₹6,000 for the daily room limit, ₹75,000 for maternity, ₹25,000 for mental health, 12 months for
pre-existing disease waiting, 9 months for maternity waiting, and 30 days for normal reimbursement filing.
These figures are meaningful only when paired with the benefit category and conditions around them.
